power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

Young people today grow up in a digital world that differs substantially from the world in which the adults in their lives grew up.

Despite this gap, young people do need guidance from adults in their lives to navigate online risks safely and to benefit from the many opportunities the digital world offers (Classen et al., 2020; Stavropoulos et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Despite this gap, young people do need guidance from adults in their lives to navigate online risks safely and to benefit from the many opportunities the digital world offers <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Classen et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Stavropoulos et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Support from adults may be especially relevant for neurodivergent youth, including those with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), mild intellectual disabilities (MID), and dyslexia (Layinka et al., 2024), as they face both heightened opportunities and elevated risks in digital environments (Alfredsson et al., 2020; Dündar & Karabıçak, 2022; El-Asam et al., 2023; Eltahir et al., 2025; Kahraman & Demirci, 2018; Stiller et al., 2019).

text.text: Youths' digital experiences are affected by commercial, aggressive, sexual, and values-related risks and educational opportunities, digital literacy learning, participation and civic engagement, creativity and selfexpression, and identity and social connection (Livingstone & Haddon, 2009; Staksrud et al., 2009).

text.text: How young people are affected by such risks and opportunities depends on individual factors such as resilience and coping, as well as broader ecological systems including families, schools and care settings (Livingstone et al., 2016).

text.text: To benefit from digital media, neurodivergent young people need knowledge and skills. Ribble (2011) describes nine interrelated elements of digital citizenship: digital access, digital literacy, digital communication, digital rights and responsibilities, digital etiquette, digital security, digital law, digital health and wellness, and digital commerce.

text.text: Together, these elements might give a first conceptual framework to help young people use digital technologies effectively, safely, and responsibly while respecting the norms, values, and rights of others.
Neurodivergent youth are typically supported through multiple systems, including education and healthcare.

Healthcare professionals and educators, henceforth referred to as 'professionals', are therefore key social agents in supporting neurodivergent young people in their digital lives (Livingstone et al., 2016).

text.text: They serve as role models and sources of information, protection and support, particularly for young people who cannot rely on parental guidance.

Professionals therefore play an important role in supporting young people to benefit from online opportunities while managing potential risks (Mendoza, 2009; Nikken et al., 2024; Nixon & Halpenny, 2010).

text.text: The online questionnaire (Phase 1) covered the domains described below.
The full questionnaire is available on request from the author.
Topics investigated were initially based on the Livingstone's (2016) framework of online risks and opportunities and Ribble's (2011) nine elements of digital citizenship.
text.formatted: Topics investigated were initially based on the <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Livingstone's (2016)</ref> framework of online risks and opportunities and <ref type="bibr">Ribble's (2011)</ref> nine elements of digital citizenship.

text.text: As the questionnaire was developed for this particular study two pilot interviews took place to check the feasibility and conceptualization of the questions.
Based on these pilot interviews only minor changes were made.
Because questionnaire items addressed distinct aspects of digital support and were analysed individually, results are presented at item level rather than as composite scales.
Capacities of neurodivergent youth.

Professionals first indicated which capacities they considered important for young people to develop, selecting from a list including digital knowledge, awareness of risks, digital skills, critical and self-aware use, and awareness of opportunities.

Next, they also rated youth's actual digital competence across nine elements of digital citizenship (Ribble, 2019), expressing their level of agreement with nine statements on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 'totally disagree' to 'totally agree'.
text.formatted: Next, they also rated youth's actual digital competence across nine elements of digital citizenship <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Ribble, 2019)</ref>, expressing their level of agreement with nine statements on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 'totally disagree' to 'totally agree'.

text.text: Professionals' own digital capacities.
Professionals rated their own digital competence using the same nine-element digital citizenship framework and response scale as above.
Support practices.

Professionals indicated which tools and approaches they used when supporting young people in digital contexts, selecting from a list including conversation skills, game-based activities, modelling, and use of websites, with the option to add other answers.
Confidence in supporting youth.

Professionals' perceived self-efficacy in supporting neurodivergent young people was measured by using the internet-specific parental self-efficacy scale (Glatz et al., 2018), adapted for use with professionals.
text.formatted: Professionals' perceived self-efficacy in supporting neurodivergent young people was measured by using the internet-specific parental self-efficacy scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Glatz et al., 2018)</ref>, adapted for use with professionals.

text.text: The scale consists of seven statements rated on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 'totally disagree' to 'totally agree'.
Professionals also indicated for which digital activities they felt confident in providing support.
Digital needs of youth.

Professionals indicated whether they received questions from young people about specific online activities, selecting from a list of topics ranging from contact with family and friends to commercial issues.
An open question addressed the nature of questions and support requested by young people.
Support needs of professionals.
For each of the nine elements of digital citizenship, professionals indicated whether they felt able to support young people independently or would like to receive support to assist the youth.
They also indicated which digital activities they could use support in when assisting young people.
Two open-ended questions asked healthcare professionals about the support they currently lacked and which questions they would like to ask a digital expert.
The focus group interviews (Phase 2) followed an open protocol based on the research question and the Phase 1 findings.

Topics included the digital needs, opportunities, and risks of neurodivergent young people, professionals' own support needs and competencies, collaboration with parents, and the impact of neurodivergence on digital behavior.
All interviews were recorded and transcribed verbatim.

In Phase 1, professionals were recruited through healthcare and educational organisations in the Netherlands, which distributed information about the study -including its aims, inclusion criteria, and a web-based link to the questionnaire -to potential participants.
The target population consisted of educators and healthcare professionals of all types who worked with neurodivergent youth aged 5 to 23 years on a daily basis.
Minor adaptations were made to the questionnaire for each subgroup, such as using the term 'student' in the version for educators and 'client' for healthcare professionals.
Inclusion criteria were verified through screening questions in the online questionnaire.
Active informed consent was obtained prior to participation.
Data collection took place between October 2024 and January 2025.
Of the 88 healthcare professionals who expressed initial interest 4 did not meet the inclusion criteria, whereas 49 provided informed consent and gave answers to the questionnaire.
In total 17 (35%) professionals completed all questions.
Of the 110 educators who expressed initial interest 1 did not meet the inclusion criteria.
63 Educators provided informed consent and responded to the questionnaire, of whom 21 (33%) completed all questions.
That means that the first topics in the questionnaire were answered by 87 professionals and only the latter ones by 38.

Given the exploratory nature of the study, all available responses were retained through pairwise exclusion to maximise the use of available data: for each topic, all available responses were included, meaning that the number of respondents varied across themes and is reported separately for each finding.

Dropout analyses revealed no significant differences between participants who completed only the demographic questions and those who completed the full questionnaire, with one exception: primary school teachers disproportionately discontinued, reporting that the questions did not align with their daily practice.

In Phase 2, convenience sampling was used to recruit participants from the researchers' professional network.

Three clinical healthcare professionals (two males and one female) working with young people with MID and four ambulatory healthcare professionals (one male and three females) working with a variety of neurodivergent young people participated.
In addition, four educators (three males and one female) at a vocational school were interviewed.

The focus group interviews took approximately one hour, with interview among clinical healthcare professionals and educators were conducted on-site at the relevant facility; interviews with ambulatory healthcare professionals were conducted online.

In the quotes presented in the results section, clinical healthcare professionals are identified as CH, ambulatory healthcare professionals as AH, and educators as E, followed by a participant number (e.g., CH1, AH2, E3).
Data collection was conducted in accordance with scientific ethical regulations.
In the questionnaire, respondents were first provided with information about the study, followed by an informed consent statement.
They indicated their consent by ticking a box before proceeding to the questionnaire.
Participants in the focus groups received information about the study and an informed consent form in advance.
They provided their consent by completing and signing the form.
The study was approved by the Research Ethics Committee of Leiden University of Applied Sciences (Reference: CEO 10/2024).
Quantitative results are descriptive and presented at item level, reporting frequencies and percentages for each question.
Where possible, confounding effects of age and professional role were examined; no significant confounding effects were found.
All focus group interviews were transcribed and analysed in Atlas.ti.
Analysis followed a sequential deductiveinductive approach (Naeem et al., 2023).

text.text: In the first round, deductive coding was applied to identify needs and capacities, using a coding scheme developed by the first author and grounded in Livingstone's (2016) framework of online risks and opportunities and Ribble's (2011) nine elements of digital citizenship.
text.formatted: In the first round, deductive coding was applied to identify needs and capacities, using a coding scheme developed by the first author and grounded in Livingstone's (2016) framework of online risks and opportunities and <ref type="bibr">Ribble's (2011)</ref> nine elements of digital citizenship.

text.text: Prior to coding, the coding scheme was discussed by the research team and minor adjustments were made to improve clarity.
Data were double-coded by two researchers; disagreements were resolved through discussion, and a third reviewer was consulted when consensus could not be reached.
Data that were relevant to the research question but not captured by the initial coding scheme were set aside during the first round and subsequently used to develop additional inductive codes.
These codes were validated by the second author and then applied in a second round of double-coding, again with disagreement resolved through discussion or third-party review.

text.text: Among educators, a substantial proportion (8-36%; 2-9 of 25) reported being unable to assess youth's digital competence for one or more elements.
Of the remaining educators, the majority also rated youth's capacities as limited across most elements.
The exception was digital literacy, where a small majority of educators (52%) agreed that students had adequate skills.
Another exception was access, for which both healthcare professionals and educators indicated that young people did not experience any difficulties.
In the focus group interviews, both groups elaborated on specific areas where youth's digital capacities were perceived as limited.
The most frequently reported concerns related to digital security, communication, etiquette, commerce, law, and wellbeing.
Professionals reported that youth have difficulties understanding official websites and official affairs.

They also suggested that youth do not always recognise the lasting consequences of their online actions and struggle with their digital footprint and tend to communicate more aggressively online than offline.

Healthcare professionals noted that disengaging from online activities can be particularly demanding for neurodivergent young people.
For example, children with autism might experience stress when they have to finish online activities, because that means the start of a new activity.
These children found it demanding to come up with new activities and to decide what to do next.
Children with ADHD might get caught up and lose control of bodily signals when playing online games.
Educators mentioned gaming as the primary concern in relation to digital health, particularly when it interferes with sleep and daily functioning.

text.text: In both groups, professionals indicated that young people need support for a range of online activities, specifically noting government affairs, school-related tasks, and searching for online information (see Appendix Table 2A).

text.text: In the focus group interviews, opportunities were discussed more extensively by healthcare professionals than by educators during the focus group interviews.
However, because opportunities were not explored using identical prompts across all groups, this discrepancy should be interpreted cautiously.

Healthcare professionals noted that digital media offers valuable opportunities for neurodivergent young people to maintain contact with classmates who attend special education schools far from their own neighborhoods.
Social media was also used by healthcare professionals themselves as a form of informal support and communication with the young people with whom they work.
Healthcare professionals noted that online communities allow neurodivergent youth to connect with others who share similar experiences, which can strengthen their sense of identity and self-esteem.
Furthermore, healthcare professionals observed that young people display online creativity and digital learning, including indirect learning through gaming.
CH3: "He is someone who looks up everything.
He is very interested in things, he googles everything, so to speak.
He suddenly comes up with all kinds of fun facts and stuff."
However, regarding digital commerce, healthcare professionals noted that while online shopping is accessible, neurodivergent young people often cannot anticipate the consequences of their purchases.
Official online services such as banking and government websites remain largely inaccessible to this group.
CH2: "You know, and also, for example, not seeing the risks: if you buy something on credit.
Then I say: 'Hey, eventually the bill will come.
You have to pay it.'"
In the focus group interviews, both healthcare professionals and educators elaborated on the types of risks neurodivergent young people encounter.
Both groups noted high levels of aggression and hate on social media.
Healthcare professionals observed that online conflicts sometimes escalate to offline violence, and that young people are exposed to harmful trends on platforms such as TikTok.
Educators similarly noted cyberbullying and hate texts as prominent risks.
E4: "Well, not all of them are nice people in the digital world, you know.
You wouldn't want to see the light of day after hearing what they say."
Both groups noted risks related to values and sexual content.
Healthcare professionals observed that young people are not selective in sharing personal information, easily connect with strangers, and find it difficult to say no.
Educators noted that despite prevention training, sharing sexual pictures without consent remains prevalent among students.
Furthermore, young people were regarded as vulnerable to commercial exploitation online, fraudulent activities, spoofing, and exploitation of personal information.
CH2: "He was involved in fraudulent practices, as you know, through online marketplaces and such, or games he had or something.
Well, he sold the same product ten times, but he never delivered it."
Both healthcare professionals and educators stated that neurodivergent young people seek more help in general compared to neurotypical young people, and that they feel less secure online.
Particularly professionals working with youth with MID mentioned that young people with MID possessed knowledge but failed to foresee risks and ignored warnings.

Educators also noted that neurodivergent students often sought help with specific practical difficulties online such as keeping an overview of websites, remembering passwords, and making typing errors that lead to problems.
However, educators reported that they had received feedback from students stating that they felt like they received too much prevention training.
This suggests that current prevention approaches are not always well-calibrated to youth's needs.
E3: "Yesterday, we had Bureau Halt [delinquency prevention officer] here…….
The theme was also cyber stuff...
I got feedback from the student council that they already knew about it.
So that shows: they do know, but exactly as you say, they need to act on it."
Professionals perceived that neurodivergent youth often understood online risks but experienced difficulties applying this knowledge in everyday situations.
Educators noted that students can reproduce prevention knowledge when asked, but struggle to apply it in real situations.
Educators felt it was nonetheless worthwhile to keep repeating key messages.
E4: "I believe that the power of repetition ultimately helps our students the most, and even if you only reach eight out of ten in the end, that's still eight more than there were before.
And maybe you'll never reach those two, but if you don't try, you'll never know."

This discrepancy between questionnaire and focus group findings among educators is noteworthy and will be addressed in the discussion.
Both groups used a range of tools and approaches when supporting young people, though with some differences in emphasis (see Appendix A Table 7A).

text.text: Healthcare professionals relied most heavily on communication techniques, while educators prioritised pedagogical skills.
Both groups made similar use of colleagues and tools.
In the focus group interviews, both groups elaborated on what these approaches look like in practice.

Healthcare professionals described predominantly using an enabling supporting style: having conversations about online issues, actively learning from young people about online language and culture -treating young people as knowledgeable about their own digital world -and playing games together with young people.
They also described offering unsolicited advice about online risks as part of everyday conversations.

Restrictive mediation was applied only rarely by healthcare professionals, though they acknowledged that neurodivergent young people do sometimes need boundaries, particularly around stopping online activities.

AH3: "Everything I didn't know about gaming and streaming and that sort of things, but over the past six months I've become so much wiser about how much money you can earn from streaming, for example, and how that works.
And I've learned a lot of new words because I'm constantly talking about that online world that is so important to some clients."
Educators similarly described an enabling approach in practice, though this was expressed more indirectly through pedagogical skills and communication techniques.
In certain contexts, particularly in relation to the school smartphone ban a more restrictive approach was described.
While educators perceived this measure as beneficial for students' wellbeing, they also noted that students often found ways to circumvent the restrictions, for example by using Chromebooks instead.
At the same time, educators emphasised the importance of respecting students' privacy and generally considered monitoring students' social media activities inappropriate.
When lacking knowledge, both groups turned to online tools, taking the quality of the source into account where possible.
Yet, when more complex problems arose, educators tended to refer to a team-manager or support-coordinator rather than handling issues themselves.
E3: "When it comes to things like online bullying, or whatever, I always forward it straight away to the teamleader."
Theme 4: Professionals' Support Needs
Despite reporting few formal support needs in the questionnaire, both groups described meaningful challenges in their day-to-day work with neurodivergent young people in the focus group interviews.
Both groups mentioned collaboration with parents as a challenge, though the nature of the challenge differed between the two groups.

Healthcare professionals described a situation in which young people are often more open with them than with their parents, leaving parents unaware of online issues and making collaboration difficult.
On top of that, when professionals were informed and wanted to share information with parents, they found it difficult to convey the urgency to parents who they felt often did not perceive the risks.
On the other hand, healthcare professionals noted that parents frequently asked for more restrictive mediation conflicting with the professionals' own approach.
AH2: "I also had a girl in my counseling program who had posted herself in her underwear on YouTube.
So I called her parents about it, and they didn't seem very impressed.
They didn't seem to realize that anyone could see it and that it could be recorded on a cell phone, meaning it could exist forever."
Educators described a somewhat more functional relationship with parents, noting that collaboration is possible when problems arise.
Privacy.
Healthcare professionals specifically mentioned young people's desire for privacy as a barrier to support.
They suggested young people could be protective of their digital worlds and resistant to professional involvement.
CH2: "Well, if you even come near it, it's gone -so to speak...
No, I think it's mainly because they just feel like: this is mine."
Responsibility and time.
Educators in particular raised questions about the boundaries of their professional role.
They described feeling that digital support falls outside their core responsibilities, and that they lack the time and specialised knowledge to address more complex digital issues.
E4: "But we are not people who ignore psychological aspects.

And you know, of course you can have conversations, but at some point that stops, and I think that as teachers we are increasingly aware that... there is a limit to what we can do, because we can all take on so much and want to solve everything, but that's not realistic.
And yes, I think ultimately you also have professional staff for that, skilled people who are more trained for that, should problems arise."
The majority of professionals in both groups reported being able to find answers when they have questions about online issues.

Both groups relied primarily on colleagues, though healthcare professionals also drew on therapists and websites, while educators made more use of student support coordinators and assisting staff (Table 5).

text.text: In the focus group interviews, both groups initially did not spontaneously identify additional support needs.
Only after explicit prompting did specific needs emerge.
Healthcare professionals identified three areas where additional support would be helpful.
First, they noted the need for more accessible official websites and government services for neurodivergent young people.
Second, they identified a need for training and interventions for parents -both to raise awareness of online risks and to help parents develop more nuanced approaches to screen time guidance.
Healthcare professionals noted that parents frequently ask for screen time guidelines but felt that a single guideline cannot be appropriate for all children.
For neurodivergent young people in particular, they believed the focus should be on managing transitions between activities rather than limiting time per se.
AH3: "I think that with autism, preparing for the end of the game is very important.

It's better to give them plenty of warning that they will have to stop gaming in a certain amount of time and to repeat this regularly so that they know when the end is coming and are prepared for it.
I think that if you do indeed give them five minutes to finish in five minutes, they will quickly become stressed."
Third, healthcare professionals identified a need for more support from management and specialists within their organisations.
Educators identified somewhat different support needs.
They noted that digital tools are helpful but should be better aligned to the emotional capabilities of neurodivergent students.
Most strikingly, educators specifically suggested the need for a dedicated digital coach -a younger professional with up-to-date knowledge of the digital landscape -to support them in their work.
E1: "But actually, you should have a youth worker or something like that, you know, someone who is 25 and still very active in the digital world and knows exactly..."

This study examined how healthcare professionals and educators perceived the digital needs, opportunities, and risks of neurodivergent youth, and how they characterised their own capacities, supporting styles, and support needs in this domain.
Professionals agreed that the digital capacities of neurodivergent youth could be strengthened, particularly in relation to applying digital knowledge in everyday situations.

Professionals perceived neurodivergent youth as technically capable and often aware of online risks, but reported that young people frequently experienced difficulties translating this knowledge into behaviour.
Furthermore, professionals acknowledged that they could not protect young people against all digital risks.
Despite initially reporting few unmet support needs, more specific needs emerged when explicitly prompted in the focus group interviews.
Key challenges identified by professionals include collaboration with parents, respecting young people's privacy, and questions about professional responsibility.

Both healthcare professionals and educators perceived the digital capacities of neurodivergent young people as limited across most elements of digital citizenship, with the notable exception of digital literacy, where educators rated students' skills more positively.

This suggests that neurodivergent youth are not uniformly lacking in digital competence (they can be technically proficient) but struggle particularly with understanding consequences, recognising risks, and navigating complex or official digital environments.
A particularly important finding concerns the gap between neurodivergent youth's knowledge about digital risks and the subsequent actions that they take.

This knowledge-action gap is consistent with previous research, which shows youth are more inclined to engage in risk behaviors in the presence of peers (Powers et al., 2022), though they may aware that their behaviour is dangerous. Kamarudding et al. (2023) have argued that school-based cyberbullying programmes typically yield small effects probably due to the challenge of translating learning into behaviour.

text.text: This suggests that prevention approaches for neurodivergent young people need to go beyond information transfer and focus more on applied, contextualised learning.
A striking asymmetry emerged between the two professional groups in how they framed digital media for neurodivergent young people.
Both professional groups attached greater importance to online risks than to online opportunities.
Yet, during the focus group interviews healthcare professionals elaborated more extensively on opportunities than educators.
However, because opportunities were not explored using identical prompts across all focus groups, differences between professional groups should be interpreted with caution.
Nevertheless, the risk-centered emphasis among educators is consistent with broader patterns in the literature.

School and policy responses to children's digital lives have historically prioritised safety and protection over empowerment and opportunity-building (Frau-Meigs et al., 2017; OECD, 2023), and digital citizenship education is frequently operationalised as responsible behaviour and online safety rather than as a balanced agenda that equally foregrounds participation, creativity, and critical engagement (Tadlaoui -Brahmi et al., 2022).

text.text: Our findings suggest that this pattern extends to educators working with neurodivergent young people, potentially leaving a gap in the support these youth receive for realising the positive potential of digital media.
Regarding risks, both groups identified aggression, commercial exploitation, and risks related to values and sexual content as prominent concerns.

These risks are not unique to neurodivergent young people, but professionals in both groups suggested that neurodivergent youth may be particularly vulnerable, for example because of difficulties in recognising social cues, saying no, or anticipating consequences.
This is consistent with existing literature on elevated online risk for young people with ADHD, autism, and MID (El-Asam et al., 2023; Eltahir et al., 2025).

text.text: Professionals reported feeling capable of supporting young people around knowledge of risks yet acknowledged that they cannot protect them against risks.
This finding might suggest the importance of equipping young people themselves with the skills and resilience to navigate digital risks, rather than relying solely on professional oversight.
That is, professionals should adopt an enabling mediation approach in young people's daily online lives rather than attempting to control their online activities (Edelaar-Peeters et al., submitted).

text.text: Both healthcare professionals and educators reported feeling reasonably confident in their own digital capacities in the questionnaire, although healthcare professionals reported to be more confident than educators.
The difference in confidence between the two professional groups may be explained in part by their different professional orientations.
Healthcare professionals approach digital support from a relational perspective, focusing on the relationship with the young person and adapting to their needs.

Educators, by contrast, may operate from a more traditional teacher-centered framework, in which the teacher is expected to be the authority on a subject before teaching it (Admiraal et al., 2017; Biggs, 2012; Serin, 2018).

text.text: In a domain as rapidly changing as digital media, this expectation of authoritative knowledge may be particularly difficult to meet, which could explain why educators feel less confident.
The different professional orientations are reflected in the supporting styles described by the two groups.

Healthcare professionals predominantly described an enabling and authoritative approach: having conversations about online issues, learning from young people about online culture, playing games together, and offering unsolicited but relationally embedded advice.
Restrictive mediation was used rarely and acknowledged as sometimes necessary but not the preferred approach.
Educators, by contrast, described a more mixed picture: their day-to-day approach was broadly enabling, but restrictive measures such as the smartphone ban were also mentioned.

This difference is consistent with broader research on digital parenting and mediation styles, which suggests that enabling and authoritative approaches are generally preferred to restrictive ones in supporting young people's digital development (Edelaar-Peeters et al., submitted; Geurts et al., 2023 , Vossen et al., 2024).

text.text: The specific challenges and needs identified differed somewhat between the two groups, reflecting their different professional roles and contexts.
Educators questioned whether digital education falls within their professional remit and expressed concern about the time and energy required.
This question is understandable.

However, the Digital Education Action plan now encourages, European member states to promote digital education in schools through clear strategic visions and concrete actions (European Commission, 2020).
In the Netherlands, new core objectives for digital education will become mandatory parts of the curriculum from August 2027 (SLO, 2025).
text.formatted: In the Netherlands, new core objectives for digital education will become mandatory parts of the curriculum from August 2027 <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(SLO, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This means that, in the near future, digital education and support will become a formal responsibility of schools and teachers.

This is only feasible if educational organisations provide clear guidelines and a student-centered approach enacting these responsibilities, so that educators experience digital education as a shared endeavour rather than an individual burden.
Privacy.
Both groups noted that young people's desire for privacy can be a barrier to digital support.
Professionals are not always permitted to monitor or restrict young people's online activities, and young people can be resistant to professional involvement in their digital lives.

One way to navigate this barrier is for professionals to maintain an open and transparent social media presence, allowing them to connect informally with young people online and gain a sense of what is happening in their digital world (Hamdiui & van den Broek, 2019).

text.text: Regularly discussing digital life as part of everyday conversations is another approach that can reduce the threshold for young people to seek support (Knipschild et al., 2025).

text.text: Healthcare professionals in particular found collaboration with parents challenging.

Parents were often unaware of online issues, tended to ask for more restrictive approaches than professionals considered appropriate, and sometimes failed to recognise the urgency of situations that professionals had identified.

This difficulty in parent-professional collaboration is not unique to the digital domain: research suggests it is a broader challenge in care for neurodivergent youth (Nikken et al., 2024; Mahboub & Yassin, 2024; Westaway, 2023).

text.text: Both groups reported using digital tools to support their work, but the selection of tools appeared relatively arbitrary.
It would be valuable to support professionals in identifying highquality, evidence-based tools.
Currently, only a limited number of evidence-based digital interventions are available (Chaplinska et al., 2026), which makes this a priority area for future development.

text.text: Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings.
First, both the questionnaire and focus group samples were recruited through convenience sampling.
In both cases, this may have resulted in samples of professionals who are more engaged or interested in the topic of digital support than average.
Additionally, dropout in the online questionnaire was substantial.
Although dropout analyses revealed no significant differences between completers and non-completers, with the exception of primary school teachers, selection bias cannot be ruled out.
Yet, the findings were combined with data from focus group interviews, providing a deeper understanding of the questionnaire responses.

Second, a discrepancy emerged between educators' questionnaire responses, in which they reported feeling digitally competent, and their focus group accounts, in which they described struggling to keep up with digital developments.

This suggests that the questionnaire may not have been well-calibrated to capture professionals' actual experiences of digital competence, and that self-report measures in this domain should be interpreted with caution.
Similarly, support needs only emerged after explicit prompting in the focus groups, raising questions about the sensitivity of the questionnaire for detecting unmet needs.

These insights seems to illustrate the importance of the mixed method approach, showing that educators might be better able to articulate their needs when they are actively considering and discussing digital opportunities and needs, at the same time one must take into account that the questionnaire is not answered by the same people who participated in the focus group interview.

Third, the broad scope of the study -covering digital capacities, opportunities, risks, supporting styles, and support needs across two professional groups -meant that not all topics could be explored in equal depth in either the questionnaire or the focus group interviews.
The mixed-methods design was chosen precisely to provide a broad overview rather than an in-depth examination of any single topic, which was appropriate given the exploratory aims of the study.
Finally, the study focused on neurodivergent youth as a broad category, without distinguishing systematically between different neurodevelopmental conditions.
Neurodivergent young people are a heterogeneous group, and findings may not apply equally across all conditions.

While comorbidity is common in this group (Godard et al., 2026; Stevens et al., 2016), this does not eliminate meaningful differences between, for example, young people with autism and those with ADHD or MID.

text.text: The digital world holds both significant opportunities and risks for neurodivergent youth, and professionals may help them to navigate both.

This study provides a first insight into how healthcare professionals and educators perceive the digital needs, opportunities, and risks of neurodivergent young people, and how they characterise their own capacities, supporting styles, and support needs in this domain.

Both groups agreed that the digital capacities of neurodivergent young people can be strengthened in specific areas, though the findings also highlight genuine strengths that should not be overlooked.
Professionals described neurodivergent youth as technically competent and generally aware of online risks, while also experiencing difficulties anticipating consequences and acting accordingly.
Support should focus less on increasing knowledge and more on helping neurodivergent youth apply existing knowledge in real-life situations.
Both groups reported feeling capable of supporting young people with digital issues in general, yet almost all acknowledged that they cannot fully protect young people against digital risks.

This underscores the importance of equipping neurodivergent young people themselves with the skills and resilience to navigate digital challenges, rather than relying solely on professional oversight.
The specific support needs of the two groups differed in ways that reflect their different roles.
Healthcare professionals reported needing support primarily in collaborating with parents and in developing nuanced, tailored approaches to guidance.
Educators reported needing support in understanding their professional responsibility for digital education and in accessing up-to-date expertise, for example through a dedicated digital coach.
Both groups would benefit from better access to high-quality, evidence-based tools and interventions for neurodivergent youth, of which currently only a limited number are available.
Finally, when making these conclusions it has to be taken into account that the study relied entirely on professionals' perceptions of neurodivergent young people's digital capacities and needs.

These perceptions may not fully reflect young people's actual experiences, and future research would benefit from combining professional perspectives with direct input from neurodivergent young people themselves.
